speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Immigration Act 1959 is the main legislation that regulates the movement of persons into and out of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since then, the landscape has evolved and there are trends that challenge our ability to exercise effective border control.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Changi Airport Terminal 5 is being built and the Johor-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link will be ready in a few years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our immigration systems must be able to manage this high and growing volume of travellers efficiently and provide a positive clearance experience while ensuring our security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The added challenge is our ageing population and shrinking workforce.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) will have to cope without a significant increase in manpower.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, the unabated security threats, including terrorism and pandemics like COVID-19, call for us to go upstream in our immigration measures, such as the collection of advance passenger and crew information and entry restrictions to be imposed on undesirable foreigners even before they arrive at our shores.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To this end, ICA has reviewed its systems and concept of operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One key initiative is the New Clearance Concept (NCC), where ICA will make good use of data analytics and automation for more secure yet efficient immigration clearance of passengers and cargo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For travellers and businesses, there will be time and cost savings from smoother and faster clearance, and for our land checkpoints, reduced traffic congestion as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is about putting in place provisions to better support and facilitate these new initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The proposals in this Bill are categorised along four broad objectives: first, to digitalise and automate immigration clearance; second, to future-proof our immigration systems and processes against new and evolving challenges; third, to strengthen our border controls; and fourth, to enhance the administration of immigration passes and permits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With automated clearance and the use of biometrics as the new norm, clause 3 of the Bill will amend section 5A of the Act to specify that a person may undergo immigration clearance using an automated clearance system, if available, but that he may also be required to appear before an immigration officer for immigration clearance after using the automated clearance system, if so directed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Biometrics will be used to create a single token of authentication that will be employed at various automated touchpoints, from bag-drop to immigration and boarding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will reduce the need for passengers to repeatedly present their travel documents at these touchpoints, allowing for more seamless and convenient processing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To this end, clause 41 expands the definition of "passenger information" and inserts a new definition of "crew information", while clause 42 expands the list of purposes in section 36B for which the Minister may authorise access to or disclosure of identifying information, passenger information and crew information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA will ensure that the data shared under this initiative will only be used for authorised purposes and that there are sufficient data privacy and security safeguards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The airport operator is also subject to the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 governing the collection, use and disclosure of personal data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second objective is to future-proof our systems and processes against new and evolving public health and security challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Advance passenger and crew information enables ICA to conduct more timely risk assessments and flag out undesirable travellers such as those who pose a public health or security threat before they reach our checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, a transport operator of a vessel, aircraft or a train that arrives, leaves or is due to leave Singapore must furnish a list of passengers and a list of crew, including their particulars, to an immigration officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA is engaging relevant cross-border transport operators on the approach for the collection and submission of advance passenger and crew information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will take their views into consideration before any new requirements are implemented.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Separate from advance information, clauses 28 to 31 amend sections 24 to 26 to allow immigration officers to require all persons to furnish particulars about themselves upon arrival.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This allows ICA to require travellers to furnish particulars such as their travel history or health status when the need arises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will remove the need for ICA to manage and remove or repatriate such individuals when they arrive in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The clause also introduces offences if a person arrives in Singapore in an in-bound conveyance despite an NBD being issued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NBD regimes have been implemented in jurisdictions such as Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The COVID-19 experience has also demonstrated the need for powers to prohibit the arrival or entry of foreigners during a pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 8 amends section 9 to clarify that the Minister is empowered to make such an order where the Minister thinks it is expedient to do so in the interests of public health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 8 also amends section 9(1A) to provide that an order made on the grounds of public security or public health can apply to persons with valid immigration permits or passes, such as Permanent Residents (PRs) or long-term pass holders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such strict measures may be necessary in a severe pandemic situation where lives are at stake.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, a person subject to an order made under section 9 is a "prohibited immigrant" under section 8(3)(o) of the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Any immigration pass or permit he holds is therefore liable to be invalidated on this ground.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 7 amends section 8(3)(o) to expressly provide that the Minister may exempt an individual from this provision so that he is not a "prohibited immigrant".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: His permit or pass will not be invalidated by the operation of section 8(3)(o), and he may return to Singapore once the order prohibiting his entry is lifted, for example, when the public health emergency has abated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, it is an offence under section 57(1)(k) of the Act for a person to make a false statement to obtain or attempt to obtain an immigration facility such as a permit or a pass.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments make clear that the applicants ultimately bear the onus of providing true and accurate information in their applications for immigration facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now speak on the third objective of strengthening border controls.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first group of amendments are on detention, custodial management, and repatriation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, immigration officers are empowered to examine persons arriving in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These persons may be denied entry for reasons such as invalid visas or expiring documents, and will be instructed to leave Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, it may take time for the necessary arrangements to be made for their departure, for example, the next available flight may be days away.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, to enhance legislative oversight over custodial management measures implemented at immigration depots, including the ICA lock-up, clause 56(c) will introduce a new section 55(1)(kb) to allow the Minister to make regulations for custodial management measures, such as medical triage and the control of unruly persons through the use of restraints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, "prohibited immigrants" are currently liable to be removed to their country of birth or citizenship, their place of embarkation, or any other port or place designated by the Controller.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it has to rely on moral suasion to do the same for the other categories of persons ordered to be removed from Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 51 will amend section 47A to rectify this anomaly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nevertheless, ICA will assess all cases carefully, and government-aided funds may be made available to help persons who are genuinely unable to afford their own repatriation expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second group of border control amendments seeks to facilitate ICA’s taking over of protective security functions from the Singapore Police Force at authorised areas such as the land checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, the Act only empowers immigration officers to stop and search persons or vehicles for immigration-related offences, or if an offence is committed within or in the vicinity of a checkpoint.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For all other cases, police officers are needed to intervene, to stop such persons or vehicles of interest, and arrest them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, clause 34 will amend section 30 of the Act to allow ICA to give instructions to all travellers arriving in or leaving Singapore, to prevent evasion of examination.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes asking travellers to queue at certain lines, or to proceed to a waiting area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, under the Act, ICA can only give instructions to arriving passengers and crew members carried in any vessel, aircraft or train.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third group of amendments pertains to immigration offenders who are either exempted from caning or found medically unfit for caning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Criminal Procedure Code 2010 provides that all females, as well as males above the age of 50 shall not be punished with caning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, caning cannot be carried out if the offender is medically unfit to undergo that punishment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such individuals can be liable for an additional imprisonment term of up to 12 months, in lieu of caning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For foreigners who commit such offences but cannot be caned, such as if they are female, keeping them in our prisons for a longer term is not in the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our aim is instead to repatriate them as soon as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Incarceration is also not an appropriate deterrent against an immigration offender whose goal is to stay in Singapore and even more so if the offender requires state-sponsored medical treatment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For such an offender, a fine, in lieu of caning, may be a more appropriate deterrent than additional jail time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is already the case for some offences in the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, for the offence of illegal entry without a valid immigration pass or permit, for which caning is mandatory, the Act requires the courts to impose fines in lieu of caning, for all females as well as males above the age of 50 who cannot be caned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, for males who were sentenced to caning, but are subsequently found medically unfit for caning, the current law does not allow the imposition of fines in lieu of caning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 8(i) of the Bill will introduce a new section 9(7), to allow the courts to also impose fines, in lieu of caning, for the section 9(6) offence of arriving, entering or remaining in Singapore in contravention of a prohibition order by using a false travel document or a travel document belonging to someone else.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This applies to all females and males above the age of 50.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The fourth type of amendment will allow ICA to better ensure a child’s safety and well-being when acting on a Restraining Order issued by a court that prevents the child from being taken out of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA already enforces such a Restraining Order when notified of it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 4 will introduce a new section 5AA that allows ICA to temporarily keep a child within the immigration checkpoint, after having prevented the child from being taken out of Singapore, until the child’s parent or guardian, or a police officer, is able to take the child into his care.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new section 5AA protects immigration officers from personal liability as long as they have acted in good faith and with reasonable care in complying with the court order or exercising this power.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Foreigners should neither be entitled nor expect to be given the right to enter or remain in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This must be the absolute prerogative of the Government acting in the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of these decisions are related to permanent residency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This aligns the treatment of such PR-related decisions with the treatment for application of immigration passes and Singapore Citizenship, for which there is no avenue of statutory appeal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although statutory appeal will no longer be available, individuals can continue to seek the Controller’s reconsideration of such decisions when there are relevant new facts or circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill also seeks to clarify at law when a PR is deemed to have lost PR status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The proposal before Parliament is specific to the scenario when the person is outside of Singapore without a valid Re-entry Permit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Entry Permit is issued when PR status is first granted and allows the person to enter and remain in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Re-entry Permit or “REP” is issued to a PR upon application and allows him to re-enter Singapore after having left Singapore temporarily; it has a fixed validity period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA deems a PR who is overseas without a valid REP to have lost his PR status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the current Act, the PR has a grace period of one month after the REP has expired to apply for an REP to reinstate his PR status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Notwithstanding this, ICA has been exercising flexibility in allowing some PRs who miss this deadline to have their PR status reinstated if they have legitimate reasons, for example, if they were hospitalised overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (a)	Clause 2 will define a “permanent resident of Singapore” as the holder of a valid Entry Permit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (b)	Clause 12 amends section 10 to provide that a non-citizen who wishes to be a PR must apply for an Entry Permit, and sets out what the Entry Permit authorises its holder to do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (c)	Clause 13 amends section 11 to require a PR who is outside Singapore without a valid REP to apply for an REP within a period to be prescribed in regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will give PRs sufficient time to remedy the situation, compared to the one-month grace period today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (d)	If the said PR applies for an REP before the end of the prescribed period, and is successful, he remains a PR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (e)	If the PR fails to apply for an REP before the end of the prescribed period, the new section 14A introduced under clause 17 provides for the automatic cancellation of his Entry Permit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will take effect on the date immediately after the last day of the prescribed period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (f)	If the PR applies for an REP before the prescribed period ends and his application is unsuccessful, this new section 14A also provides that his Entry Permit will be automatically cancelled, and this will take effect on the date immediately after ICA has rejected the REP application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (g)	Clause 13 introduces section 11(2A) to clarify that the Controller may refuse the grant of REP to a PR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Each REP application is subject to a polycentric evaluation of factors relating to our policies and security, the PR’s period of residence in Singapore, his contributions to Singapore, family ties and conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If a person who has lost PR status wants to be a PR again, he will need to make a fresh application for PR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We encourage all PRs to obtain an REP or to renew their expiring REP in a timely manner, before travelling out of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The vast majority of REP applications are approved as long as the PR continues to be committed and contribute to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes retired PRs because we recognise that while they may no longer be earning an income, they had contributed to Singapore during their working years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of those who are unsuccessful in applying for an REP to reinstate their PR have far exceeded the existing grace period for reinstatement despite the flexibility exercised by ICA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The rest do not live in Singapore anymore, no longer have family ties to locals here, are no longer contributing economically or have adverse records.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, ICA must first notify permit holders of any such changes in conditions and invite them to make representations in this regard before such changes take effect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 12 and 13 amend sections 10 and 11 to allow such changes in conditions to be effected simply through the giving of notice to the affected permit holders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 56 updates the Minister’s regulation-making powers, such that similar provisions may be introduced to provide the Controller with similar powers in respect of immigration passes and certificates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These provisions will allow ICA to impose new conditions on permit, pass and certificate holders especially during a contingency such as a pandemic, as well as to regulate the conduct of the holders more efficaciously through the variation of existing conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last, the Bill also makes other technical, related and consequential amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA has been relying solely on the Immigration Act since the 1980s to remove undesirable foreigners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is no operational impact, and the provisions under the Banishment Act can be found in other legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is imperative for Singapore’s safety and security, and to maintain our status as a world-class transport hub and destination.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is well known that our ICA officers, staff and auxiliary police officers deployed at our immigration checkpoints have heavy workloads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These officers often make personal sacrifices to discharge their duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Owing to the lean manpower situation, they frequently forgo going on leave during school holidays which coincides with the peak travel periods.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is so that fellow Singaporeans are not inconvenienced when they travel on holidays.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They deserve our salute for steadfastly securing Singapore’s borders and keeping us safe despite the significant challenges, some of which were enunciated by the hon Second Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the manpower crunch that all sectors across Singapore face, it makes eminent sense to leverage on technology to ease the clearance process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The plans to implement automated and contactless clearance and the checkpoints without passport presentation are particularly welcome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only will these measures result in faster clearance, but they also improve the experience of travellers too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these reasons, I fully support the provisions in the Bill to implement the automated and contactless clearance process at checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the other objectives of the Bill, I seek clarification on three broad areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the face of it, the replacement of a prison term imposed in lieu of caning with fines instead of imprisonment alone may dilute the overall deterrent effect of the sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the policy reason for this is to reduce the state resources that would otherwise be committed when foreigners who cannot be caned have to serve longer imprisonment terms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In principle, I do not have an issue with the policy so long as the execution of this policy is carefully calibrated with other sentencing aims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One, why is this policy applicable to an offender convicted of the offence of employing five or more illegal immigrants under the proposed section 57(1B) of the Act?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Usually, such offenders, being employers, are likely to be Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the policy precipitating this change should not be applicable to this class of offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Two, why is there no provision in the Bill to deal with the probability that immigration offenders do not pay the fine?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would imagine that most foreign immigration offenders would lack the means to pay fines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is why they left their home to come to Singapore – to make money.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If fine sentences are imposed in lieu of imprisonment over the inability to carry out a caning sentence, we would have to deal with the high probability that these offenders would not be able to pay the fine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such a situation, since nothing is specifically proposed in the Bill, section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code, or CPC, would apply.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This provision gives the Court the power to impose an additional imprisonment term in default of payment of fine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a scale under section 319 of the CPC that determines the limit of the imprisonment terms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For offences punishable with a term of 24 months or more, the maximum imprisonment term cannot exceed half of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the upper limit of the scale.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For offences punishable with imprisonment for a term less than 24 months, the maximum imprisonment term cannot exceed one-third of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the lower limit of the scale.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are several offences provided in the Immigration Act that are subject to caning, for which the upper limit under section 319 of the CPC applies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And to illustrate that, if you were to look at section 9 of the Act as it currently stands, which deals with an immigration offender who has already been issued with a Prohibition Order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If he were to come into Singapore again, then, he may face an imprisonment term of not less then two years or not more than five years, and shall also be liable to be fined and caned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, a simple provision in the amendment Bill would have taken care of this – spelling out that a shorter imprisonment period, or the lower limit under section 319 of the CPC may be imposed in situations where fines, imposed in lieu of caning, are not paid.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would term this as an issue of fairness in dealing with foreigners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In explaining this provision, I note the hon Minister's point: entry into Singapore is really the prerogative of the government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Respectfully, I am concerned about these proposals for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, from a values perspective, I disagree with the view that just because we are dealing with foreigners who should not expect the right of entry or stay in Singapore, we should deal with them summarily.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, our immigration system should reflect the values we stand for as a nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Granted, we do not owe non-Singaporeans the same duties and obligations we owe to ourselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But foreigners should have the same recourse to justice, as a matter of principle, and in this case, we owe them two specific duties as members of a common humanity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To mandate that they need not be told why they are labelled as prohibited immigrants, nor offer them an avenue to provide explanation does not, in my respectful view, fulfil this duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, we must be mindful that a good number of foreigners who may be subject of action by the Controller have spousal or familial relations with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such affected Singaporeans would certainly expect that the system operates fairly for their spouses or relatives in dealing with immigration matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I said on point of fairness, sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would imagine if the roles were reversed, Singaporeans who are immigrants in other countries would expect to be dealt with fairly by foreign immigration authorities too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current appeal process to the Minister ensures that there will be no single point of failure; from a system perspective.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should be mindful it is proposed in this Bill that the Controller be vested with even more powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As was explained by the hon Minister, one example is the No Boarding Directive to deny foreigners from boarding from places of embarkation, even as transit travellers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just by having an appeal process alone, we will ensure, system-wise, that the Controller will use his powers carefully and with circumspection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By having an appeal process, the Minister would be able to have access to all relevant facts of the case to make his own decision on the merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is as opposed to a mere administrative review by the Minister on the basis that ICA comes under his charge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is well capable of handling sensitive factors and information too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, this is the rationale for providing the statutory appeal to the Minister instead of to the Court which is ordinarily be accessible by members of public and the press.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate that the Government must be pragmatic in dealing with immigration matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, unlike some countries which deal with immigration matters through the judicial system and have a backlog of cases to handle, I do not think a similar situation exists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister’s explanation to my concerns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this area, I wish to raise two points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The provisions in the Bill, as they stand, are to be wide enough to include public transport operators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should they apply, however, this may create practical problems and bottlenecks having regard to the huge number of train and bus commuters that the operators will have to handle on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second and finally, I note that it is proposed that the Controller be vested with the power to temporarily restrain a child from leaving Singapore in compliance with the court order until the child’s parent or legal guardian collects him or her.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from my professional colleagues who practise family law that, in the usual case, the Family Court would order that a child be allowed to leave Singapore where the other parent provides his or her written consent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such orders would then be served on ICA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: ICA will then have to take on the obligation to operationalise the order by checking to see if the "suitable person" wanting to bring the child out of Singapore has the requisite written consent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if there is scope to digitalise the entire process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They should cover both the notification of Court orders as well as the lodgement of written consent with ICA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, I believe we will gain more efficiency and reduce the risk of making mistakes, too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill will introduce provisions to support ICA's new clearance concept to further automate immigration clearance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate that ICA is in the forefront of immigration technology.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But I have three concerns to highlight regarding the rollout of the NCC.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some categories of travellers frequently face difficulties in the process of clearing immigration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, some elderly citizens are unable to provide usable fingerprints due to their dry skin.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Wheelchair users may have difficulty getting their irises scanned due to the height and angle of the scanners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Iris recognition systems could become prone to error as people's irises change with age or after cataract surgery and the biometrics of young children are still developing and may change over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the NCC include reasonable accommodations, like wider gates for wheelchair users and adjustable scanners that can capture biometrics from travellers who cannot hold their head up for long?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most importantly, will special assistance lanes which are manned by ICA officers continue to be provided at the passenger halls of Changi Airport and all land and sea checkpoints and will they be easily accessible by all travellers with special needs?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, I note that the Bill empowers the Minister to authorise the disclosure of passenger information to the airport operator for specific uses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does this airport operator refer to only the Changi Airport operator or also operators of foreign airports?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Do the specific uses include sharing of Singaporeans' biometric data?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What enhanced safeguards are in place to ensure data security, particularly if Singaporeans' data will be shared with third-party vendors or foreign governments over which we have little control?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And third, I note that Singapore is one of the first countries in the world to implement NCC-type capabilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another key area of amendments in the Bill is to enable ICA to more efficiently administer immigration passes and permits issued to foreigners and PRs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Cross-national marriages between a Singaporean and a foreigner make up about a quarter of all marriages in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Foreign spouses face many challenges settling down in Singapore, the chief of which is obtaining permission from the Government to remain in Singapore for a long term.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be achieved first through securing a Long-Term Visit Pass or LTVP and, subsequently, a PR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For foreign spouses who hold university degrees and draw high salaries, obtaining a LTVP, PR and even citizenship is usually not difficult since their income and skills add great weight to their applications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But those with low educational qualifications and incomes face far greater challenges in obtaining long-term residency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At my Meet-the-People Sessions, which are attended mainly by residents in the lower-income groups, about a fifth of cases involve immigration matters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Singaporean residents who approached me are usually disappointed that their foreign spouses' LTVP or PR applications were unsuccessful and want me to make appeals for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some shared with me their deep longing to start a family but their hesitation due to their spouses' uncertain immigration status.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most do not understand why the applications were rejected because no reasons are provided by ICA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During a 2012 parliamentary exchange between Ms Indranee Rajah and the then-Minister of State Mr Masago Zulkifli, Ms Rajah highlighted three cases of Singaporeans with prior convictions who are facing difficulties getting their foreign spouses' LTVP approved.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Masagos agreed with Ms Rajah that families are the pillar of support for ex-offenders but clarified that family, in this case, referred to an existing family unit, not a new family unit formed when an ex-offender got married soon after his release.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He added that an offender just out of prison has many issues to deal with and an environment he is not familiar with anymore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He further stated that should a marriage not work out or the husband re-offend, the spouse, who is a foreigner, will not have relatives in Singapore to turn to nor jobs to sustain herself or her children as many are, generally, low-skilled.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many may be estranged from their existing families or may have suffered divorce while incarcerated and are starting anew.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, having a spouse provides stability and an added incentive for them to remain crime-free.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should not deny ex-offenders who have served out their prison sentence the right to get married to anyone they choose to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, once they are married, it would be most unfair for the state to deny or delay a foreign spouse's long-term residency on account of the ex-offender's past conviction.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could put a strain on their marriage and finances and keep the ex-offender "locked" in a second prison.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should not make it difficult for a married couple to stay together by denying an LTVP to a foreign spouse or child of a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Family formation is one of the core social values in Singapore and our immigration policy must support it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my conversations with residents who face difficulty getting an LTVP for their foreign spouses, most were unaware of the PMLA before they tied the knot.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the Registry of Marriages (ROM) and the Registry of Muslim Marriages advise cross-national couples to complete the PMLA before getting married?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that the ROM website advises them to undergo a PMLA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, is this highlighted to the couple in person before the marriage registration process, keeping in mind that many of these couples may not be proficient in reading English?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, even passing the PMLA is not a guarantee of obtaining an LTVP after marriage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister explained that not every person who has obtained a letter of LTVP eligibility goes on to apply for an LTVP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But it is unclear if this fully accounts for the 37% gap.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has stated in this House that ICA generally does not disclose the reasons for unsuccessful applications for immigration facilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This lack of transparency is out of step with the practices in some other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Canada, for spouse sponsorship applications that are refused, their government provides reasons for refusal in writing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, Australia's Department of Home Affairs explicitly states that if a partner's visa application is refused, the department will provide information on why the visa was refused.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I wish to propose four approaches that could improve ICA's immigration process for the immediate family members of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, there should be disclosure of the broad reasons for rejection of LTVP, PR and citizenship applications by foreign spouses, children and parents of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They do not have an easy option to settle in another country if their spouse is not given permission to live with them in Singapore for the long term, especially if they are from a lower-income group.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When rejections happen without a reason, the Singaporean spouse can feel disconnected from their own nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have seen this in the eyes of my constituents who sought appeals for immigration applications for their spouses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, where mitigation paths for future applications can be furnished, ICA should do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, if an applicant was rejected because their economic contributions were not deemed sufficient, they should be informed of this so that they can take steps to enter the workforce, upskill themselves and strive to perform better at work so as to earn promotions and salary increments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is preferable over an opaque dead end.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Previous answers by Ministers in this House have revealed the range of factors that are considered for LTVP, PR and citizenship applications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why not list all these criteria clearly on the ICA website and on application forms instead of expecting applicants to comb through the Parliament Hansard?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Applicants meeting these criteria should get fast-track approval with discretionary rejections allowed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister told this House in 2018 that ICA does not share the specific criteria or grounds for rejecting applications due to concerns that information about detailed assessment criteria can be abused to inflate an undeserving applicant's chances of success and that some people could then try to game the system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in presenting the COMPASS framework, which is used to evaluate foreigners' employment passes and went live this month, the Government emphasised that it brings benefits like transparency, clarity and predictability for businesses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: COMPASS provides a points system, specific benchmarks for salaries and diversity and employs objective data so that firms can actually assess where they stand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the COMPASS criteria spell out in no uncertain terms how many points are awarded for various factors, like salary, qualifications and improving diversity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) is comfortable with the disclosure and transparency in the COMPASS framework in order to provide businesses with clarity and predictability for manpower planning, then surely, ICA can also extend these same principles to Singaporeans and their foreign spouses, children or parents who need the same clarity and predictability for their family planning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also said that the reasons for rejection may be used to arouse negative sentiments in other countries and that this may create bilateral sensitivities and is not in Singapore's interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In any case, ICA does not need to tell the applicant that they were rejected because they were from a particular country or a particular race.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If there are reasons for rejection that may conceivably cause diplomatic friction, those need not be shared with the applicant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the vast majority of reasons for immigration rejections are not going to sour relations with other country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us not throw out the baby with the bath water.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, ICA should provide clearer channels for immigration appeals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have no objection to the removal of this right.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I agree that foreigners have no right to demand to enter or stay in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The website only states that failed PR applicants may submit a fresh application if there are changes to their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, residents often tell me that they were advised by ICA officers to make an appeal through their Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I am grateful for the chance to engage more of my residents at my Meet-the-People Sessions, submitting appeals through one's Member of Parliament should not be the default means of communication between citizens and the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They could lessen the anxiety and frustration that Singaporeans with foreign spouses, children and parents experience with the immigration process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Following the challenges posed by the global pandemic, it is heartening to note that all our checkpoints are once again bustling with activity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The numbers crossing our checkpoints speak volumes about our nation's economic resilience and quick recovery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proposed legislation demonstrates our commitment to utilising technology and digitalisation to enhance ICA’s operations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments seek to improve efficiency and productivity within our immigration processes, whilst upholding stringent controls to ensure that the right individuals enter Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, on digitalisation and, next, on the self-declarations by passengers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have clarifications on data security and operational issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The adoption of the NCC, prompts us to consider its impact on the future of passports and its associated data security measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share how many countries have also employed such technologies regularly to allow for seamless travel?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the implementation of such technologies eventually render physical passports irrelevant?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would be insightful to understand if the ICA envisions a time when passports might be phased out in favour of e-passports.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the ICA plan to collaborate with other Government agencies like GovTech, Cyber Security Agency and Smart Nation Digital Government Group (SNDGG) to raise the resilience of our digital solutions against potential scammers and frauds?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore’s passport is highly sought after, any vulnerabilities and breaches in the system can result in the theft of critical passenger data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does ICA intend to address the needs of individuals who might not be digitally adept and ensure that no one is left behind in this transformative journey when residents use the NCC?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, the retention period of passenger data and the mechanisms to safeguard it are of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could ICA shed light on how long personal data will be stored?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, will there be a designated timeframe for the destruction of this information?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What rigorous measures are in place to prevent hacking or misuse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could we receive assurance on how personal data, particularly biometrics, will be fortified against potential breaches?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister clarify the exemption status of operators like SBS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister also provide insights into the rationale behind this exemption?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about taxis and coaches which operate across our borders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, understanding the potential challenges faced by transport operators in complying with this new clause is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans for a transition period to facilitate a smooth implementation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When can we expect the composition framework to be introduced to support transport operators?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, how can we address the concerns of passengers who are worried that some of these bus companies lack the necessary infrastructure to secure their personal data?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the projected short- and long-term impacts of allowing digital permits and passes on the flow of travellers at these checkpoints?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will ICA address situations where individuals may not possess a functional electronic device to present e-permits?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will physical permits still be issued or remain valid as an alternative option?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, let us proceed to issues concerning self-declaration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With regard to the offence of making false statements, how does ICA plan to effectively monitor and validate the accuracy of these declarations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could ICA provide insights into the frequency of validation or fact-checking procedures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to implement audit checks to ensure the compliance and accuracy of these self-declarations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we all know, strong enforcement serves as one of the most effective deterrents against such transgressions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does ICA plan to strengthen enforcement measures to discourage false statements and uphold the sanctity of self-declarations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is a concern that new diseases are not accurately declared.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we consider the potential health risks posed by contagious diseases, a pertinent scenario arises: if a passenger fails to declare symptoms of a new disease, or is ignorant of the symptoms, how would ICA issue a no-boarding directive or prevent such a passenger from disembarking in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does ICA intend to collaborate with MOH to address this concern?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With limited resources and space, we must be vigilant in managing the entry of individuals into our country.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's allure as a destination for visitors and foreigners is well-recognised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, our attractiveness also renders us susceptible to criminal elements, due to the significant influx of people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While preventing acts of terrorism is a primary concern, there is an additional facet to consider.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I suggest that we use technology to further differentiate different categories of control measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This represents an important step forward to optimise productivity, especially in a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, our manpower is precious and limited.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must be able to assess what we want to achieve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They pave the way for Singapore to remain open and innovative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are fully prepared to meet the challenges and opportunities ahead.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The integration of cutting-edge methods, such as biometrics and data analysis, into our immigration processes improves security and overall travellers' experience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed amendments enable the ICA to achieve greater operational efficiencies from future-proofing against new and evolving challenges, digitalise and automate immigration processes, strengthening border controls and efficient administration of immigration passes and permits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, on future-proofing against new and evolving challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would unify the ICA’s powers to do so across all modes of entry, as entry into Singapore via buses is not covered under the Immigration Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is no reason why entry by bus should be considered less of a security threat compared to entry by air or sea.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This unification of security measures gets us closer to completing our nation’s security infrastructure to collecting information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It prevents such individuals from travelling to Singapore in the first place, instead of only being turned back at our checkpoints on arrival.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are four points that I would like to highlight for the Ministry’s consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Human errors or technological glitches are realities in any operational system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Strict liability offences do not account for genuine mistakes or errors made in judgement made by transport operators.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, Singapore's reputation as an international transportation hub depends not only on security measures but also on its ability to facilitate smooth travel for passengers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Overly harsh penalties for transport operators could deter them from serving Singapore, potentially reducing our attractiveness as a transit point for travellers and cargo.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I call on the Ministry to consider to strike a balance between our objective of making Singapore an international transport hub and safeguarding our security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, it is currently proposed for NBDs to cover individuals who are both entering and transiting in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that there is, indeed, value for NBDs to apply to transit passengers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore cannot become an easy transit point for undesirable characters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share how many instances of undesirable characters that have transited through our checkpoints in recent years and how these could have been avoided if we had NBDs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on the electronic service of giving notices of NBDs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry clarify how long in advance does the controller need to inform operators that an NBD is issued in relation to a passenger or crew they are ferrying?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, I would like to call on the Ministry to provide operators with a suitable transition timeframe to ensure compliance with NBDs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must ensure that operators have sufficient time to adjust their operational design and workflow to comply with NBDs without unduly impacting their other business objectives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, on the proposed amendments which grants ICA officers the authority to require travellers to furnish particulars about themselves upon arrival.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As currently proposed, this power may be exercised by ICA officers to furnish particulars about themselves “as that officer may require”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will guide officers in their duties and also passengers in their adherence to the requests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Given the current security environment, increased travellers’ demands, and the nation’s ageing workforce, there is a pressing need for secure and streamlined immigration clearance procedures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The NCC aims to automate routine tasks and allocate human resources to more critical functions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share if manpower and operational workstreams are ready for the NCC?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, what is the net impact on the ICA officers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can they be trained and upskilled for a smooth transition?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps we can redeploy affected ICA officers to other roles with higher human touch, or even providing courses for upskilling to help ICA officers transition into working alongside the NCC effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the Ministry has stated that this data will be retained for a “short time” with adequate “safeguards”, there may still be concerns about the necessity and potential risks associated with holding such sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are also constantly at risk of cyber-attacks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the cyber-security provisions to ensure the integrity of the NCC?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the contingency plans during data breaches?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In recent months, there has also been significant delays at our immigration checkpoints due to technological glitches.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry and the ICA stepping up to prevent such incidents?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could share the measures we are taking to prevent a system-level breakdown like the one we suffered as recent as March 2023.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: ICA personnel currently possess the ability to make arrests for non-immigration violations occurring within or near authorised zones and detain vehicles for immigration-related infractions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When non-immigration violations beyond authorised areas are identified at checkpoints, ICA relies on police officers to effect arrests or detentions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By updating the Act, Singapore demonstrates its commitment to effective border management while embracing technology in line with our digital nation blueprint and greater operational efficiencies at our borders.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We expect 12 to 14 million visitors this year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the same period, we had close to 1.2 million cruise passengers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At Tuas and Woodlands land checkpoints, daily crossings are around 300,000 to 400,000 people.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: An efficient, effective and resilient border control is critical to smoothen the movement of people and restrict criminals and blacklisted travellers from coming into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the increasing number of visitors, juxtaposed against a shrinking workforce, the use of technology to automate immigration clearance is a critical enabler.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Advance technology will improve the speed of immigration clearance and enhance security.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Digitalisation and automation will enable ICA to make efficient use of limited manpower resources.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: ICA is one of the early adopters of facial recognition technology.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: When Changi Airport Terminal 4 opened in October 2017, the Automated Immigration Gates allowed Singaporean passengers to sail through immigration clearance without the need to interact with an ICA officer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The shift to the automated clearance by using facial recognition and fingerprint for identity validation was a major milestone then.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: ICA has extended the automated clearance to foreigners as well.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Instead, they can use the Automated Border Control System with their biometrics for clearance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the NCC, immigration clearance will become even faster and smoother for all travellers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, the amendments to the Bill will enhance ICA's powers to obtain information on travellers upstream.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The introduction of NBDs will require transport operators to deny the boarding of undesirable individuals that are a threat to our security.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Screening them prior to arrival and prohibiting them from arriving or transiting is a necessary step towards the protection for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The benefits of faster and easier immigration clearance and manpower savings are evident.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, the typical pitfalls associated with digitalised and automated systems must also be highlighted and the mitigation measures carefully considered.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The first relates to system reliability and their massive knock-on effects.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The system must be made extremely robust to prevent system breakdowns, long down time and false negatives, which will all result in delays in clearance, resulting in build-up of long queues and passengers missing their flights, and other knock-on effects.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Sometime in March this year, there were delays and long queues at Changi Airport and land checkpoints.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This disruption to the immigration clearance system lasted more than five hours.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will the NCC be more resilient to such breakdowns?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One, how can ICA prevent or minimise the occurrences of such failures?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What measures does ICA have in place to protect and reinforce the systems?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two, will the Ministry have regular independent audits to check on the failure rates?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Three, what are the contingency plans since manning levels will be minimal with the implementation of NCC?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Four, how quickly can the back-up response kick in?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I do hope that there are sturdy solutions to address these technical weaknesses and operational impacts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The second concern relates to cybersecurity and biometric vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Despite cybersecurity protection, hacking incidents and data breaches continue to affect both private companies and public organisations more often than expected.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In 2021, there was a data leak affecting 580,000 Singapore Airlines' customers, arising from an external air transport information technology company.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Last year, personal information of 4,749 KrisShop customers were exposed to a phishing attack.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For the departure process, the NCC entails an end-to-end biometric system to be used to verify identities and travel details at various automated touchpoints, from bag-drop, to immigration and to boarding.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This would mean that the travellers’ biometric information will be stored and linked to even more points than we have today.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Though this process will provide more convenience, will the trade-off result in an increase in a higher risk exposure to data breaches?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Internationally, the number of public and private organisations collecting and keeping biometric information has been increasing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Correspondingly, the number of hacking incidents involving biometric data is also on the rise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Given this trend, how will the Ministry ensure the strictest protection for biometric data?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unlike passwords, we must be mindful that in the event of data breaches, biometric data such as fingerprints and iris scans cannot be reset.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can we assure Singaporeans, residents, and travellers of their concerns over the collection of their biometric information is a safer option compared to traditional identification methods?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am also concerned about the credentials and quality of IT contractors’ systems and staff when it comes to outsourced technology work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How robust are the checks on theses contractors and the background clearance of their staff?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the potential vulnerabilities from the involvement of foreign partners, firms and governments?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, are these IT systems contracted out to firms with foreign associations?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My third concern is about small private bus operators.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Understandably, these bus operators will not have the means to validate such information.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should not burden the bus operators on immigration matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's immigration has been one of the most user-friendly anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This latest Bill will make it even easier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Two of these changes, namely the advanced clearance for conveyances and for cargo, are likely to make a big difference in our land borders with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, is it envisioned that foreign nationals coming through these land borders will also be able to take advantage of these automated clearance measures?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I definitely think these measures will increase the speed of clearance at customs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One concern that arises from this though is whether these changes will make checks become less stringent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In particular, does it mean that customs officials may not check people, vehicles and cargo for most vehicles passing through these checkpoints, or are there alternative automated methods for checking vehicles, cargo and passengers?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am also interested to know whether ICA intends to share data and information with other governments which may make automated clearance possible for foreigners in Singapore, and for Singaporeans abroad?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The sharing of data may also be made consensual, meaning that frequent travellers who prefer to clear customs more quickly may consent to their data being shared with governments of countries they regularly visit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may be especially useful once the RTS Link between Singapore and Johor starts operating.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If a good part of this traffic switches to the RTS, that may have the benefit of reducing vehicles and road congestion in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, this option will become especially attractive if customs' clearance is automated for regular daily travellers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may mean that travel from Singapore to Johor may one day be only a little bit more difficult than taking an MRT.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of the other changes in this Bill include giving ICA officers the powers they need to prevent undesirable people from entering Singapore, including provisions giving them the power to detain, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The requirement for pre-clearance of passengers on board aircrafts and vessels also allow ICA to prevent undesirable people from boarding these vessels if they wish to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are sensible measures and I think better for everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, the only way to prevent these people entering Singapore is after they have already arrived but before they have cleared Customs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means that individual concerns may have to be detained and repatriated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This step will be avoided if pre-clearance can be done.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One area of concern for me is how permanent residents (PRs) are being dealt with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill sets out a legal basis for people who may lose the PR status and also it removes the avenue of appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To better understand the people being affected, I would be interested to know and I have a few clarifications here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second – how many of these would appeal against such loss?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, of those that appealed and failed, how many would take up the avenue to appeal to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And fourth, I know this last one may be a bit sensitive, how many such appeals have succeeded?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think these questions will give us a sense of how many people will be affected by the changes and the extent of that effect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand the rationale for these changes is to make clear the basis for losing PR and the removal of the avenue for appeal to Minister is to harmonise the avenues for appeal for other foreigners such as employment pass and long-term visit pass holders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, I think people have generally regarded the PR status as being much more important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, though, I think this Bill makes important exciting changes to our immigration process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most Singaporeans can expect even more seamless and convenient travel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the right of appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill removes the statutory right of appeal against certain decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: ICA’s website appears to provide no information on how to request for such reconsideration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify by what channels should PR applicants and PRs request ICA’s reconsideration of its decisions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What should such requesters provide and how long should they expect to wait for a response?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will ICA consider providing a standard form for filing such requests?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would centralise ICA’s intake of requests and reduce administrative complexity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This form could also provide information about factors relevant to ICA’s reconsideration and warn against the inclusion of irrelevant documents and submission of frivolous requests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would likely cut the time taken to review requests and reduce the volume of requests, saving Government resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For this category of decisions, MHA has not stated that these individuals can seek ICA’s reconsideration of its decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify whether individuals who are subject to decisions on removal from Singapore, and entry and re-entry permits can seek ICA’s reconsideration?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If yes, what is the process for seeking ICA’s reconsideration?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the variation of conditions of entry permits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that entry conditions are important for the legality of stay in Singapore, can Minister share when it would not be practicable to give notice to every individual?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will individuals with no knowledge of prescribed websites and no habit of reading the Gazette learn about the variation of conditions of their entry permits?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is about how children will be prevented from being taken out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A new section 5AA states that an immigration officer may prevent a child from leaving Singapore or being taken out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, the immigration officer may keep the child in an authorised area.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can be a traumatising situation for a child.
